claim: Both generalized arousal and engagement in a specific task influence sensory neural processing.
source: Both generalized arousal and engagement in a specific task influence sensory neural processing.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general premise of the study.

claim: Single-unit activity was recorded from primary auditory cortex (A1) and inferior colliculus (IC) of ferrets during a tone detection task.
source: To isolate effects of these state variables in the auditory system, we recorded single-unit activity from primary auditory cortex (A1) and inferior colliculus (IC) of ferrets during a tone detection task, while monitoring arousal via changes in pupil size.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Arousal was monitored via changes in pupil size.
source: To isolate effects of these state variables in the auditory system, we recorded single-unit activity from primary auditory cortex (A1) and inferior colliculus (IC) of ferrets during a tone detection task, while monitoring arousal via changes in pupil size.
evidence: This describes the method used to measure arousal in the study.

claim: A generalized linear model was used to assess the influence of task engagement and pupil size on sound-evoked activity.
source: We used a generalized linear model to assess the influence of task engagement and pupil size on sound-evoked activity.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Task engagement and pupil size affected independent neural populations in both A1 and IC.
source: In both areas, these two variables affected independent neural populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in the manuscript.

claim: Pupil size effects were more prominent in IC than in A1.
source: Pupil size effects were more prominent in IC, while pupil and task engagement effects were equally likely in A1.
evidence: This is a primary finding comparing the two brain regions.

claim: Pupil and task engagement effects were equally likely in A1.
source: Pupil size effects were more prominent in IC, while pupil and task engagement effects were equally likely in A1.
evidence: This is a primary finding about A1 neural responses.

claim: Task engagement was correlated with larger pupil size.
source: Task engagement was correlated with larger pupil; thus, some apparent effects of task engagement should in fact be attributed to fluctuations in pupil size.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between task engagement and pupil size.

claim: Some apparent effects of task engagement should be attributed to fluctuations in pupil size.
source: Task engagement was correlated with larger pupil; thus, some apparent effects of task engagement should in fact be attributed to fluctuations in pupil size.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between task engagement and pupil size.

claim: There is a hierarchy of auditory processing where generalized arousal enhances activity in midbrain and effects specific to task engagement become more prominent in cortex.
source: These results indicate a hierarchy of auditory processing, where generalized arousal enhances activity in midbrain, and effects specific to task engagement become more prominent in cortex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the differential effects observed in IC and A1.

claim: Engaging in a task that requires auditory discrimination leads to changes in neural excitability, as well as in spectral and spatial selectivity.
source: Compared to passive listening, engaging in a task that requires auditory discrimination leads to changes in neural excitability, as well as in spectral and spatial selectivity (Downer et al., 2015; Fritz et al., 2005; Fritz et al., 2003; Knudsen and Gentner, 2013; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Lee and Middlebrooks, 2011; Otazu et al., 2009; Ryan and Miller, 1977; Yin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to temporal expectation.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jaramillo and Zador, 2011.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to reward associations.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beaton and Miller, 1975 and David et al., 2012.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to self-generated sound.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Eliades and Wang, 2008.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to motor planning.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bizley et al., 2013 and Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to motor activity.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schneider et al., 2014 and Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to degree of engagement.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carcea et al., 2017 and Knyazeva et al., 2020.

claim: Task-related changes in neural activity have been attributed to behavioral choice.
source: Task-related changes in the activity of auditory neurons have been attributed to temporal expectation (Jaramillo and Zador, 2011), reward associations (Beaton and Miller, 1975; David et al., 2012), self-generated sound (Eliades and Wang, 2008), and non-sound related variables, such as motor planning (Bizley et al., 2013; Huang et al., 2019), motor activity (Schneider et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014), degree of engagement (Carcea et al., 2017; Knyazeva et al., 2020), and behavioral choice (Tsunada et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tsunada et al., 2016.

claim: Fluctuations in neural activity are observed throughout the forebrain, including primary sensory regions, even in the absence of explicit behavior.
source: Even in the absence of explicit behavior, fluctuations in neural activity are observed throughout the forebrain, including primary sensory regions (Ringach, 2009; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ringach, 2009 and Stringer et al., 2019.

claim: Pupil size has been shown to correlate with mental effort in humans.
source: In humans, luminance independence changes in pupil size have been shown to correlate with mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Winn et al., 2015), changes in states of arousal (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966), aspects of decision-making (Gilzenrat et al., 2010), and task performance (Schriver et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Beatty, 1982 and Winn et al., 2015.

claim: Pupil size has been shown to correlate with changes in states of arousal in humans.
source: In humans, luminance independence changes in pupil size have been shown to correlate with mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Winn et al., 2015), changes in states of arousal (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966), aspects of decision-making (Gilzenrat et al., 2010), and task performance (Schriver et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kahneman and Beatty, 1966.

claim: Pupil size has been shown to correlate with aspects of decision-making in humans.
source: In humans, luminance independence changes in pupil size have been shown to correlate with mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Winn et al., 2015), changes in states of arousal (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966), aspects of decision-making (Gilzenrat et al., 2010), and task performance (Schriver et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gilzenrat et al., 2010.

claim: Pupil size has been shown to correlate with task performance in humans.
source: In humans, luminance independence changes in pupil size have been shown to correlate with mental effort (Beatty, 1982; Winn et al., 2015), changes in states of arousal (Kahneman and Beatty, 1966), aspects of decision-making (Gilzenrat et al., 2010), and task performance (Schriver et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schriver et al., 2018.

claim: Fluctuations in pupil size closely track locomotion and neural activity throughout the mouse forebrain.
source: In animals, fluctuations in pupil size closely track locomotion and neural activity throughout the mouse forebrain (McGinley et al., 2015; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McGinley et al., 2015 and Stringer et al., 2019.

claim: Pupil size tracks the degree of neural synchronization observed in local field potentials.
source: Pupil size also tracks the degree of neural synchronization observed in local field potentials, which is commonly used to measure arousal (Schwartz et al., 2020; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schwartz et al., 2020 and Vinck et al., 2015.

claim: Four adult ferrets were trained on a go/no-go auditory detection task.
source: To study interactions between pupil-indexed arousal and task engagement, we trained four adult ferrets on a go/no-go auditory detection task (David et al., 2012; Yin et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental subjects and task used in the study.

claim: Animals reported the presence of a target tone following a random number of broadband noise reference stimuli.
source: Animals reported the presence of a target tone following a random number of broadband noise reference stimuli (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the task structure, with reference to Figure 1A,B.

claim: Animals were required to withhold licking a water spout during the reference sounds.
source: They were required to withhold licking a water spout during the reference sounds and were given liquid reward for licking during the target window (0.1–1.5 s after target onset).
evidence: This describes the behavioral requirements of the task.

claim: Animals were given liquid reward for licking during the target window (0.1–1.5 s after target onset).
source: They were required to withhold licking a water spout during the reference sounds and were given liquid reward for licking during the target window (0.1–1.5 s after target onset).
evidence: This describes the reward structure of the task.

claim: All animals performed consistently above chance after training.
source: After training, all animals performed consistently above chance (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding about behavioral performance, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Mean pupil size was consistently larger during the active condition compared to passive condition.
source: Mean pupil size (measured by the major axis diameter) was consistently larger during the active condition (n = 35 sites total, ferret L: n = 13, B: n = 5, R: n = 16, T: n = 1, p = 0.0133, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding about pupil size differences between conditions, supported by statistical test and Figure 1D.

claim: Average pupil size was similar for false alarm (FA) and hit trials.
source: Average pupil size was similar for false alarm (FA) and hit trials, but it was smaller during miss trials, more closely resembling passive trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding about pupil size across different trial types, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Average pupil size was smaller during miss trials, more closely resembling passive trials.
source: Average pupil size was similar for false alarm (FA) and hit trials, but it was smaller during miss trials, more closely resembling passive trials (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding about pupil size during miss trials, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: During behavior, trial onset evoked a rapid increase in pupil size, which was consistently larger than any evoked change during the passive condition.
source: During behavior, trial onset evoked a rapid increase in pupil size, which was consistently larger than any evoked change during the passive condition (p = 4.00 x 10−6, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 1E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding about pupil dynamics during behavior, supported by statistical test and figures.

claim: Pupil size tracked slow changes in task-engagement (active versus passive blocks).
source: Thus, pupil size tracked slow changes in task-engagement (active versus passive blocks) as well as more rapid changes in trial-by-trial performance during the active condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil size data.

claim: Pupil size tracked more rapid changes in trial-by-trial performance during the active condition.
source: Thus, pupil size tracked slow changes in task-engagement (active versus passive blocks) as well as more rapid changes in trial-by-trial performance during the active condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pupil size data.

claim: 129 units were recorded from A1.
source: We recorded extracellular spiking activity from A1 (n = 129 units total, ferret B: six sites/88 units, R: one site/13 units, T: one site/28 units) and IC (n = 66 units total, ferret B: four sites/7 units, L: 13 sites/46 units, R: 10 sites/13 units) of ferrets, while they switched between active engagement and passive listening.
evidence: This describes the sample size for A1 recordings.

claim: 66 units were recorded from IC.
source: We recorded extracellular spiking activity from A1 (n = 129 units total, ferret B: six sites/88 units, R: one site/13 units, T: one site/28 units) and IC (n = 66 units total, ferret B: four sites/7 units, L: 13 sites/46 units, R: 10 sites/13 units) of ferrets, while they switched between active engagement and passive listening.
evidence: This describes the sample size for IC recordings.

claim: 18 units were recorded from central IC (ICC).
source: In the IC, we recorded from central (ICC, n = 18 units) and non-central regions (NCIC, n = 48 units), distinguished by their functional topography (Slee and David, 2015).
evidence: This describes the sample size for ICC recordings.

claim: 48 units were recorded from non-central IC (NCIC).
source: In the IC, we recorded from central (ICC, n = 18 units) and non-central regions (NCIC, n = 48 units), distinguished by their functional topography (Slee and David, 2015).
evidence: This describes the sample size for NCIC recordings.

claim: 66/129 (51%) A1 units showed a significant increase in r2 for the full model over the null model.
source: Across the entire data set, 66/129 (51%) A1 units and 37/66 (56%) IC units showed a significant increase in r2 for the full model over the null model, indicating an effect of either task engagement or pupil size (p < 0.05, jackknife t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding about the proportion of A1 units showing state-dependent modulation, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: 37/66 (56%) IC units showed a significant increase in r2 for the full model over the null model.
source: Across the entire data set, 66/129 (51%) A1 units and 37/66 (56%) IC units showed a significant increase in r2 for the full model over the null model, indicating an effect of either task engagement or pupil size (p < 0.05, jackknife t-test; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding about the proportion of IC units showing state-dependent modulation, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The full model showed consistent improvement over the null model in both A1 and IC.
source: A comparison of variance explained across the entire data set shows consistent improvement by the full model over the null model in both A1 (mean r2 null: 0.282, full: 0.340, p < 10−5, hierarchical bootstrap test, Saravanan et al., 2020) and IC (mean r2 null: 0.290, full: 0.399, p < 10−5, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding about model performance, supported by statistical tests and Figure 3B.

claim: About a quarter of state-dependent A1 units showed unique pupil-dependent modulation (15/66).
source: Although the proportion of units with any significant state-related modulation was comparable between A1 and IC, only about a quarter of those A1 units showed unique pupil-dependent modulation (15/66), compared to about a half for IC (20/37).
evidence: This is a finding about the proportion of A1 units with pupil-dependent modulation.

claim: About half of state-dependent IC units showed unique pupil-dependent modulation (20/37).
source: Although the proportion of units with any significant state-related modulation was comparable between A1 and IC, only about a quarter of those A1 units showed unique pupil-dependent modulation (15/66), compared to about a half for IC (20/37).
evidence: This is a finding about the proportion of IC units with pupil-dependent modulation.

claim: In A1, the variance explained by task (mean r2 task-unique: 0.017) was significantly greater than variance explained by pupil (mean r2 pupil-unique: 0.007, p = 0.0335, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: In A1, the variance explained by task (mean r2 task-unique: 0.017) was significantly greater than variance explained by pupil (mean r2 pupil-unique: 0.007, p = 0.0335, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding about the relative contributions of task and pupil in A1, supported by statistical test and Figure 3C.

claim: In IC, the variance explained was not significantly different between task and pupil (mean r2 task-unique: 0.016, mean r2 pupil-unique: 0.019, p = 0.769).
source: In IC, the variance explained was not significantly different between task and pupil (mean r2 task-unique: 0.016, mean r2 pupil-unique: 0.019, p = 0.769).
evidence: This is a finding about the relative contributions of task and pupil in IC, supported by statistical test.

claim: There was a significant correlation between d' and the unique variance explained by task in A1 (r2 task-unique; r = 0.303, p = 0. 007, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: Indeed, we found a significant correlation between d' and the unique variance explained by task in A1 (r2 task-unique; r = 0.303, p = 0. 007, hierarchical bootstrap; Figure 4A, left).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between behavioral performance and task-related neural modulation in A1, supported by statistical test and Figure 4A.

claim: There was no correlation between d' and the unique variance explained by task in IC (r = 0.069, p = 0.318).
source: The same relationship was not observed in IC (r = 0.069, p = 0.318; Figure 4A, right), nor was there a relationship between d' and unique variance explained by pupil in either area (r2 pupil-unique; A1: r = 0.113, p = 0.158; IC: r = −0.017, p = 0.552, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of relationship between behavioral performance and task-related neural modulation in IC, supported by statistical test and Figure 4A.

claim: There was no relationship between d' and unique variance explained by pupil in A1 (r = 0.113, p = 0.158).
source: The same relationship was not observed in IC (r = 0.069, p = 0.318; Figure 4A, right), nor was there a relationship between d' and unique variance explained by pupil in either area (r2 pupil-unique; A1: r = 0.113, p = 0.158; IC: r = −0.017, p = 0.552, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of relationship between behavioral performance and pupil-related neural modulation in A1, supported by statistical test and Figure 4B.

claim: There was no relationship between d' and unique variance explained by pupil in IC (r = −0.017, p = 0.552).
source: The same relationship was not observed in IC (r = 0.069, p = 0.318; Figure 4A, right), nor was there a relationship between d' and unique variance explained by pupil in either area (r2 pupil-unique; A1: r = 0.113, p = 0.158; IC: r = −0.017, p = 0.552, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of relationship between behavioral performance and pupil-related neural modulation in IC, supported by statistical test and Figure 4B.

claim: Accounting for pupil size led to a 33% reduction in the magnitude of MIAP in both A1 and IC.
source: Effectively, accounting for pupil size led to a 33% reduction in the magnitude of MIAP in both areas (A1: mean magnitude MIAP task-only = 0.141; MIAP task-unique = 0.095; IC: MIAP task-only = 0.069; MIAP task-unique = 0.046).
evidence: This is a finding about the effect of accounting for pupil size on task-related modulation.

claim: The effect of removing pupil-related activity on the magnitude of active versus passive modulation was not different between central and non-central regions of IC (ICC versus NCIC, p = 0.467, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: The effect of removing pupil-related activity on the magnitude of active versus passive modulation was also not different between central and non-central regions of IC (ICC versus NCIC, p = 0.467, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the consistency of pupil effects across IC subregions, supported by statistical test and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a negative correlation between task-unique and pupil-unique modulation in A1 (r = −0.281, p = 0.040, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: We found a negative correlation between these quantities in A1 (r = −0.281, p = 0.040, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 6, left) and no correlation in IC (r = 0.104, p = 0.191, Figure 6, right).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between task and pupil modulation in A1, supported by statistical test and Figure 6.

claim: There was no correlation between task-unique and pupil-unique modulation in IC (r = 0.104, p = 0.191).
source: We found a negative correlation between these quantities in A1 (r = −0.281, p = 0.040, hierarchical bootstrap, Figure 6, left) and no correlation in IC (r = 0.104, p = 0.191, Figure 6, right).
evidence: This is a finding about the lack of relationship between task and pupil modulation in IC, supported by statistical test and Figure 6.

claim: The frequency of joint occurrences of task and pupil effects was no greater than expected for independent distributions in both A1 (p = 0.41) and IC (p = 0.59).
source: The frequency of joint occurrences was no greater than expected for independent distributions in both areas (A1: p = 0.41, IC: p = 0.59, permutation test).
evidence: This is a finding about the independence of task and pupil effects, supported by permutation test.

claim: In A1, MIAP task-only was positive on average (median 0.069, p = 0.0240, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: In A1, MIAP task-only, computed without accounting for effects of pupil, was in fact positive on average (median 0.069, p = 0.0240, hierarchical bootstrap).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of task-related modulation in A1, supported by statistical test.

claim: In A1, MIAP task-unique was not significantly different from zero (40/69 positive, median MIAP task-unique = 0.027; p = 0.232).
source: However, MIAP task-unique, which accounted for pupil size, was not significantly different from zero (40/69 positive, median MIAP task-unique = 0.027; p = 0.232).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of task-unique modulation in A1, supported by statistical test.

claim: In IC, average MIAP task-only was not different from zero (MIAP task-only median: −0.010, p = 0.310).
source: In IC, average MIAP task-only was not different from zero (MIAP task-only median: −0.010, p = 0.310), but MIAP task-unique showed a trend toward being negative (17/49 positive, median: −0.037; p = 0.062).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of task-related modulation in IC, supported by statistical test.

claim: In IC, MIAP task-unique showed a trend toward being negative (17/49 positive, median: −0.037; p = 0.062).
source: In IC, average MIAP task-only was not different from zero (MIAP task-only median: −0.010, p = 0.310), but MIAP task-unique showed a trend toward being negative (17/49 positive, median: −0.037; p = 0.062).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of task-unique modulation in IC, supported by statistical test.

claim: The average effect of increased pupil size was positive in A1 (55/69 positive, median MILS pupil-unique = 0.0139, p = 0.032, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: In contrast to the variable task-related effects, the average effect of increased pupil size was positive in A1 (55/69 positive, median MILS pupil-unique = 0.0139, p = 0.032, hierarchical bootstrap).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of pupil-related modulation in A1, supported by statistical test.

claim: In IC, there was a trend toward increased firing rate with larger pupil (31/49 positive, median MILS pupil-unique = 0.022; p = 0.090).
source: In IC, there was also a trend toward increased firing rate with larger pupil (31/49 positive, median MILS pupil-unique = 0.022; p = 0.090).
evidence: This is a finding about the direction of pupil-related modulation in IC, supported by statistical test.

claim: In IC, but not in A1, units that responded less reliably to sound showed greater dependence on state (A1: r = −0.134, p = 0.130; IC: r = −0.323, p = 0.0129, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: In IC, but not in A1, units that responded less reliably to sound also showed greater dependence on state (A1: r = −0.134, p = 0.130; IC: r = −0.323, p = 0.0129, hierarchical bootstrap; Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between auditory responsiveness and state-dependence, supported by statistical test and Figure 7.

claim: In both A1 and IC, the magnitude of firing rate modulation between passive blocks was significantly reduced after accounting for effects of pupil (A1: p < 10−5, IC: p < 10−5, hierarchical bootstrap).
source: In both A1 and IC, the magnitude of firing rate modulation between passive blocks was significantly reduced after accounting for effects of pupil (A1: p < 10−5, IC: p < 10−5, hierarchical bootstrap).
evidence: This is a finding about the effect of accounting for pupil on post-behavior effects, supported by statistical test.

claim: Accounting for pupil size led to a 20% reduction in P1 versus P2 modulation in A1.
source: Accounting for pupil size led to a 20% and a 48% reduction in P1 versus P2 modulation in A1 and IC, respectively (A1: mean signed-normalized MIP1P2 block-only = 0.140, MIP1P2 block-unique = 0.100; IC: mean signed-normalized MIP1P2 block-only = 0.100, MIP1P2 block-unique = 0.052).
evidence: This is a finding about the effect of accounting for pupil on post-behavior effects in A1.

claim: Accounting for pupil size led to a 48% reduction in P1 versus P2 modulation in IC.
source: Accounting for pupil size led to a 20% and a 48% reduction in P1 versus P2 modulation in A1 and IC, respectively (A1: mean signed-normalized MIP1P2 block-only = 0.140, MIP1P2 block-unique = 0.100; IC: mean signed-normalized MIP1P2 block-only = 0.100, MIP1P2 block-unique = 0.052).
evidence: This is a finding about the effect of accounting for pupil on post-behavior effects in IC.

claim: Some post-behavior effects previously reported as persistent plasticity induced by behavior can be explained by fluctuations in pupil size.
source: Thus, while some post-behavior effects previously reported as persistent plasticity induced by behavior can in fact be explained by fluctuations in pupil size, a small number of units showed persistent post-behavior changes, even after accounting for pupil.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of post-behavior effects.

claim: A small number of units showed persistent post-behavior changes, even after accounting for pupil.
source: Thus, while some post-behavior effects previously reported as persistent plasticity induced by behavior can in fact be explained by fluctuations in pupil size, a small number of units showed persistent post-behavior changes, even after accounting for pupil.
evidence: This is a finding about persistent post-behavior effects that cannot be explained by pupil size.

claim: Pupil-indexed arousal and task engagement operate via distinct feedback circuits.
source: However, these changes affected independent neural populations, suggesting that effects of pupil-indexed arousal and other aspects of task engagement operate via distinct feedback circuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that task and pupil affect independent neural populations.

claim: Pupil-related changes occurred in both A1 and IC.
source: Pupil-related changes occurred in both areas, but task engagement effects were more prominent in A1.
evidence: This is a summary finding about the distribution of pupil effects across brain regions.

claim: Task engagement effects were more prominent in A1 than in IC.
source: Pupil-related changes occurred in both areas, but task engagement effects were more prominent in A1.
evidence: This is a summary finding about the distribution of task engagement effects across brain regions.

claim: All procedures were approved by the Oregon Health and Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol IP1561).
source: All procedures were approved by the Oregon Health and Science University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol IP1561) and conform to National Institutes of Health standards.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Four young adult male ferrets were obtained from an animal supplier (Marshall Farms, North Rose, NY).
source: Four young adult male ferrets were obtained from an animal supplier (Marshall Farms, North Rose, NY).
evidence: This describes the source of experimental subjects.

claim: Constant luminance was maintained throughout the experiment so that fluctuations in pupil size reflected only changes in internal state.
source: Constant luminance was maintained throughout the experiment so that fluctuations in pupil size reflected only changes in internal state (McGinley et al., 2015; Schwartz et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes an experimental control to ensure pupil size reflects internal state rather than light changes.

claim: Cholinergic fibers projecting to A1 from the nucleus basalis play a key role in rapid switching between passive listening and active engagement by modulating the activity of different populations of cortical inhibitory interneurons.
source: Cholinergic fibers projecting to A1 from the nucleus basalis play a key role in rapid switching between passive listening and active engagement by modulating the activity of different populations of cortical inhibitory interneurons (Kuchibhotla et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kuchibhotla et al., 2017.

claim: The activity of cholinergic and noradrenergic terminals in A1 was found to be elevated during pupil dilation and reduced during pupil constriction.
source: In addition, the activity of cholinergic and noradrenergic terminals in A1 was found to be elevated during pupil dilation and reduced during pupil constriction (Reimer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Reimer et al., 2016.

claim: The correlation between task engagement and pupil size could be explained by shared cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling.
source: Thus, these neuromodulatory systems have been implicated in effects of both task engagement and pupil-indexed arousal. The correlation between these state variables could be explained by shared cholinergic and noradrenergic signaling.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the correlation between task engagement and pupil size.
